storylines.label: Reasoning Latent
storylines.latest_title: [AINews] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai

editorial.tldr: An Oct 18 paper proposed hybrid agents that reason in latent space but act through text. A paper on Oct 27 then applied latent reasoning to multi-agent systems by storing reusable skills in compact external memory.
editorial.whats_new: No new latent-reasoning research landed after Oct 30; the Nov 4 item is a Latent Space newsletter that matched on name only, so the thread is still three unreplicated preprints.
editorial.why_it_matters: Latent reasoning aims to cut inference cost by keeping intermediate steps out of text, but it also makes those steps harder to inspect and log.
editorial.take_for_builders: These are unreplicated preprints; if you log reasoning traces for debugging, check what your tooling would lose before adopting latent-reasoning models.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Verda Inference, in Preview with Kimi K3.1 Pro

editorial.tldr: Kimi K3.1 started as a pre-release name tangled in China's proposed export-license rule, then was benchmarked against Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Moonshot launched K3.1 Pro on Oct 24, and a quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting.
editorial.whats_new: vLLM shipped day-0 support for Kimi K3.1 Pro on Nov 4, and Verda opened a preview of its inference service serving the model the same day.
editorial.why_it_matters: Self-hosting is now practical on vLLM, and K3.1 Pro is on several third-party clouds, so you can price it against first-party quotas, which Moonshot had to reset after launch complaints.
editorial.take_for_builders: Pin the vLLM version before self-hosting K3.1 Pro and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing. Keep a second host as fallback, since the first-party quotas failed at launch.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro has moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to vLLM support and several third-party hosts; independent quality and cost data are still thin.

storylines.label: MCP Servers
storylines.latest_title: AI coding agents are installing abandoned MCP servers with known security issues

editorial.tldr: On Nov 1 a benchmark post reported a 17-point gap between agents running the same model across 21 MCP servers. On Nov 2 a Show HN project proposed cryptographic agent identity and Uber described an MCP Gateway governing 800+ servers.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 4 write-up reports AI coding agents installing abandoned MCP servers with known security issues, adding supply-chain risk to the thread on agent-side MCP trust.
editorial.why_it_matters: MCP trust now has three open fronts: which client runs the server, which identity it presents, and which servers an agent is allowed to install at all.
editorial.take_for_builders: Allowlist MCP servers instead of letting coding agents pick them, audit installed servers for abandonment and known advisories, and pin the agent client alongside the model in MCP evals.

status.detail: Agent variance, identity and gateway governance are now joined by reports of agents installing vulnerable servers.

storylines.label: DeepSeek Open-sources
storylines.latest_title: DeepSeek Open-Sources Super-Agent, a Coding Agent That Works From Team Chat

editorial.tldr: DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer on Oct 20, the inference software behind its production models, first framed as a way to cut AI operating costs and then as pressure on OpenAI and Anthropic. Oct 21 coverage added the 155T tokens-a-day serving scale and a high serving margin.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 4: another outlet repeats that DeepSeek's Super-Agent coding agent works from team chat; still no independent results or license detail.
editorial.why_it_matters: Two open DeepSeek releases in two weeks, a serving stack and a coding-agent architecture, give platform teams reference designs to benchmark their own inference and agent harness against.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read the DeepInfer and dsh-superagent repos and licenses before borrowing designs; treat the margin and bug-fixing claims as unverified until someone reproduces them outside DeepSeek's stack.

status.detail: DeepInfer is public and unreproduced; dsh-superagent is described as a research prototype with no independent results yet.

storylines.label: GPT-6.1 Sol
storylines.latest_title: DevRev delivers autonomous self-service with GPT-6.1 Sol

editorial.tldr: GPT-6.1 Sol surfaced on Oct 15 as the new Codex CLI default, reported at 77% lower cost by a third-party site. OpenAI then began publishing customer case studies on it, starting with CodeRabbit's security agent on Oct 26.
editorial.whats_new: OpenAI's Nov 4 DevRev case study says GPT-6.1 Sol powers its Computer and Operator agents for enterprise self-service, citing the reasoning, speed and cost balance.
editorial.why_it_matters: Sol is moving from a coding-tool default into production agents for security review and customer service, so its cost and latency now matter beyond Codex.
editorial.take_for_builders: Rerun your own agent evals on Sol and compare cost per task before switching defaults; the 77% figure comes from a third-party site, not OpenAI.

status.detail: Evidence so far is vendor case studies plus one unverified third-party cost claim; no independent benchmark is in the thread.

storylines.label: MoE Inference
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: MoEShift - Faster large MoE inference with half the RAM

editorial.tldr: An Oct 27 arXiv paper framed edge MoE inference as an expert-weight movement problem rather than a compute problem. Two Hacker News posts followed within a week, showing the same memory constraint being attacked on a single DGX Spark and on Macs.
editorial.whats_new: A Show HN project (Nov 3) claims faster MoE inference on a Mac with less RAM, following a Nov 2 post on running a 124B MoE on one DGX Spark.
editorial.why_it_matters: MoE models only fit small hardware if expert weights are moved or compressed cleverly, so memory footprint, not FLOPs, decides which models you can serve locally.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you plan local MoE serving, benchmark peak memory and expert-load traffic on your target hardware before trusting parameter-count estimates.

status.detail: Research and hobbyist projects converge on memory-bound MoE inference on small hardware.

storylines.label: Learning Through
storylines.latest_title: MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution

editorial.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of agentic-RL papers, not one developing story. Since Oct 19 it has gathered research-state search training, memory-skill learning, and a study of when fine-grained credit assignment helps or hurts.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 3: MDSKILL, an arXiv paper, internalizes skill memory into agent weights through multi-view on-policy self-distillation, complementing RL for self-evolving agents.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent RL is shifting from prompt-held memory toward training signals: MDSKILL distills skill memory into the policy, and the Oct 26 credit-assignment study warns finer signals do not always help. All are paper-reported results, not production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you keep skill memory in prompts, rerun your evals against a distilled variant before committing, and A/B fine-grained credit against episode-level reward; treat all of these results as unreplicated.

status.detail: A loose set of agentic-RL papers; the newest moves skill memory from the prompt into the model via self-distillation.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks

editorial.tldr: This thread was regrouped from a broad 'large language models' reading list into reinforcement learning. Oct 15-23 papers centered on agentic RL environments, rollout budgets and credit assignment, with an AWS SageMaker guide for multi-turn RL.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 2-3: three more RL papers, including JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent framework for long-horizon web tasks, and EffComp, which trains prompt compression with RL.
editorial.why_it_matters: Nearly all of this is research: the recurring cost levers are rollout budgets, scheduling and credit assignment, which decide what agent RL training costs and whether it is stable.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you train agents with RL, try rollout-budget or scheduling ideas on your own cost curve and rerun your evals; treat these preprints as unreplicated until code and independent results appear.

storylines.label: Learning Long-Horizon
storylines.latest_title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks

editorial.tldr: Mid-October arXiv papers began framing long-horizon agent work around research-state tracking and continual-learning benchmarks. Late October added search evaluation with failure localization, critic-based credit assignment, and memory governance.
editorial.whats_new: JHiMA-WebRL applies joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning to long-horizon web tasks, following a paper questioning whether long-horizon terminal benchmarks are actually deep.
editorial.why_it_matters: Long-horizon failures (lost state, stale memory, weak credit assignment) are what break production agents; this cluster shows research moving from raw task length toward diagnosing where trajectories fail.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you evaluate long-running agents, track failure nodes and memory staleness rather than turn counts alone; these are unreplicated preprints, so rerun on your own tasks before adopting any method.

storylines.label: Qwen 3.8
storylines.latest_title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

editorial.tldr: Qwen 3.8 coverage began as benchmark claims for the 27B open-weight build. In mid-October, OrcaRouter published comparison pieces setting Beam 1.0, Glimpse and Dory 1.0 4B against it.
editorial.whats_new: On Nov 3, Simon Willison reported that Qwen 3.8 27B running on his laptop can interpret model weights, tied to the Sparks of Weight-Space Programming paper.
editorial.why_it_matters: Qwen 3.8 27B is now a baseline other vendors position against, and a laptop-sized open model is being used for weight-level interpretability experiments.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you use Qwen 3.8 27B locally, rerun the weight-reading experiment on your own checkpoint before relying on it, and treat vendor comparison posts as unverified until they cite benchmark scores.

status.detail: Qwen 3.8 appears mostly as a comparison point, with one new hands-on interpretability result.

storylines.label: Same Different
storylines.latest_title: Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?

editorial.tldr: Most of this thread shares a "Same X, Different Y" title pattern, not one event. Three arXiv papers (Oct 22-26) cover chemistry identifier binding, credit assignment for agentic RL and news framing; a Nov 1 post then reported a 17-point gap between agents using one model.
editorial.whats_new: On Nov 3, an IBM Research Hugging Face post compared CUGA, Hermes and Deep Agents on the same model, a day after an arXiv audit showed multimodal benchmark graders can change scores on identical outputs.
editorial.why_it_matters: Harness posts and the grader audit point the same way: scores depend on the agent harness and the scoring rule as much as the model, so evaluate the full stack, including how answers are graded.
editorial.take_for_builders: Hold the model fixed and vary the harness in your own eval on your MCP servers, and pin and review your scoring rule; treat the 17-point figure and IBM's CUGA comparison as vendor or blog results until reproduced.

status.detail: Title-match papers are coincidental; the Nov 1 and Nov 3 posts plus the Nov 2 grader audit form the real thread on non-model variance in evals.

storylines.label: Visual Language
storylines.latest_title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models

editorial.tldr: Mid-October arXiv papers extended multimodal LLMs with tool use and reasoning-driven embeddings. Late October work turned to when models should refuse and how vision and language modules exchange information.
editorial.whats_new: VIGOR, an arXiv preprint, orders token unmasking by visual gain to reduce hallucination in multimodal discrete diffusion language models.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multimodal failures, such as answering without enough visual evidence or losing perception under small perturbations, are reliability issues for any pipeline that feeds images to a model.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you ship vision inputs, add an insufficient-evidence refusal case and a perturbed-image case to your evals; these preprints are unreplicated, so verify on your own data.
